# Explicit Managed Update

`yantra browser update` replaces the Yantra-managed Chrome for Testing installation with the current
Stable build, after you accept the exact build being installed. It is also the only place in Yantra
that ever asks whether a newer browser exists.

## What It Does

### Answers the update question, and is the only thing that does

Nothing else in Yantra resolves Chrome for Testing metadata — not startup, not `run`, `resume`,
`ask`, `research`, or `do`, not the recorder, `init`, `doctor`, `browser list`, `browser use`, or
`browser check`, and not the scheduler, the daemon, or a nested `workflow_run`. There is no
schedule, no reminder, no background probe, and no model-visible capability to trigger one.

Nothing records that a check happened, either. There is deliberately no `lastCheckedAt` timestamp, no
availability cache file, and no update-interval or retained-version configuration key — a stored
timestamp is the seed of the background checking this feature exists to avoid. A resolved build, the
comparison, and the availability report are per-invocation memory only.

### Reports availability without changing anything

`yantra browser update --dry-run` resolves current Stable, compares it against the recorded managed
build, prints the verdict, and stops. It takes no lock, needs no acceptance, and cannot download,
install, replace, launch a browser, publish a ready pointer, write configuration, or reclaim disk.

Because it owns nothing, it is not blocked by anything: a running managed browser and an in-progress
operation are reported as local state rather than treated as refusals.

The mode is spelled `--dry-run` because `yantra config data-dir --dry-run` already owns that spelling
for "report what this would do without doing it". It is deliberately not spelled `--check`:
`browser check` in the same command group already means a local compatibility probe with no network,
which is the opposite operation. For the same reason `--dry-run --yes` is refused as conflicting
modes — an acceptance flag on a command that changes nothing is a control that does nothing.

### Replaces the installation after consent that names the build

Mutation mode checks local preconditions before paying for anything. It requires an existing managed
installation, and it refuses while a managed browser is running, naming the owning process IDs.
Both refusals happen before any metadata request, because discovering a busy machine after a 200 MB
transfer is a wasted download.

Stable is then resolved exactly once, before you are asked, and never re-resolved afterward. The
consent record names that exact build and the build it replaces, and the update is refused if the
two ever disagree — so a new Stable published mid-operation cannot substitute itself for what you
approved. Consent comes from `--yes` or an affirmative terminal prompt; a JSON or non-interactive
invocation without `--yes` fails with an actionable error rather than hiding a prompt.

Acquisition then runs through the same transaction `yantra browser install` uses. There is one
acquisition path in the product, not two: the same preflight, the same owned helper process, the
same candidate layout, the same executable verification, the same isolated capability probe, and the
same atomic publication. Immediately before publishing, the update re-verifies that no managed
browser has started during the transfer.

### Never downgrades, and never silently no-ops

Three verdicts are successes that exit `0`:

- **up-to-date** — the installed build is current Stable. No lease, no download, no prompt.
- **installed-newer** — the installed build is newer than current Stable. Both identities are
  reported and the installation is left alone. Yantra does not downgrade.
- **replaced** — the new build was verified and published.

Build ordering comes from the pinned `@puppeteer/browsers` comparator, never a string comparison.
This is not a detail: compared as text, `153.0.8010.36` sorts before `153.0.8010.9`, which would
report a real update as a downgrade and silently refuse it.

A `capability-checked` compatibility pairing is reported as ordinary provenance, never as a warning.
Chrome ships Stable faster than Yantra bumps its driver, so a build outside Puppeteer's tested
pairing is the normal state, and a warning that is always on is a warning nobody reads.

### Leaves the previous browser working through every failure

Any failure, refusal, or cancellation before publication leaves the ready pointer untouched and the
previous installation selected, launchable, and usable offline. The failed and cancelled outcomes
carry the surviving installation so the command can say so plainly. A metadata, proxy, or network
failure is an update failure only; it never renders an installed browser unusable.

There is no transaction phase machine, no recovery routine, no resume, and no user-visible "your last
update did not finish" state. The design makes one unnecessary: publication is a single atomic
pointer write, and any `installation-*` child the pointer does not name is an orphan. A killed update
leaves an orphan; the next explicit `install` or `update` collects it and reports the bytes
reclaimed. Orphans are never selectable, because selection reads the pointer.

## How to Use It

```bash
# Is a newer browser available? Changes nothing.
yantra browser update --dry-run
yantra browser update --dry-run --json

# Replace the managed installation.
yantra browser update          # prompts on a terminal
yantra browser update --yes    # required for --json or a non-TTY
```

Human notices and bounded progress always go to stderr. With `--json`, stdout carries exactly one
newline-terminated `browser_update` envelope, marked `dryRun: true` or `dryRun: false` the same way
`config data-dir` marks its dry run.

A replacement envelope reports the outcome, the previous and new build ids, the executable path, the
managed root, the compatibility verdict and its pairing, the orphan counts and bytes reclaimed, and
the selection notice. Raw helper stderr, archive command lines, environment contents, and proxy
credentials are never emitted.

The command registers no `--browser` or `--browser-path`: it always operates on the managed
installation and could not honor a per-invocation selection, so it rejects those flags as unknown
rather than accepting a control it would ignore.

### Exit codes

| Exit | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| ---: | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
|  `0` | Replaced, already up to date, or the installed build is newer than Stable                                                                                                                           |
|  `1` | `--dry-run --yes`, an unsupported flag, missing `--yes` under `--json` or a non-TTY, or consent naming a different build                                                                            |
|  `3` | No managed installation, a managed browser is running, another operation holds the lease, or a classified metadata, proxy, network, host, helper, extraction, compatibility, or publication failure |
|  `4` | You declined the prompt, or the replacement was cancelled                                                                                                                                           |

Every environment failure names what was observed and one supported repair, and no two failure codes
render identical text.

## Behavior Details

### Coordination

Busy is checked twice. `hasActiveUse()` is consulted before any metadata call, and the exclusive
mutation lease is claimed — which re-checks under the coordination mutex — before the replacement
phase, with a final re-verification immediately before publication. Once the lease is held, a new
managed launch refuses with `operation-in-progress` through the existing resolution contract, so the
download window has nothing to race against.

A running managed browser is never terminated to make room for an update, and the command never waits
indefinitely for one to exit. Uncertain process liveness fails conservatively: the update refuses
rather than authorizing a deletion it cannot prove is safe. External browsers and their launches are
unaffected throughout, and no external installation is ever written to or deleted.

### Network and proxy

The single metadata request runs in the same owned Node helper process the installer uses, spawned
with a fixed environment allowlist and `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1`. This matters because the underlying
browsers package treats proxy support as an optional dependency and silently sends requests direct
when it is absent — a bypassed proxy that no error would reveal. A proxy-routed failure is reported
as a typed proxy error naming the host with credentials stripped.

In resolve mode the helper asks for the Stable tag — never `latest`, never a release channel — tests
whether the artifact is downloadable for the host platform, answers, and exits. It is given no cache
directory, and creates no directory and writes no file anywhere.

### Storage

A replacement writes only inside the Yantra-owned managed root. The new build occupies its own
`installation-<opaque-id>` child, disjoint from the one it replaces, and the ready pointer is moved
onto it atomically. Nothing is promoted or renamed in place, the managed root and the coordination
directory are never deleted, and no common ancestor of the old and new installations is ever removed.
Executable paths are recomputed from recorded relative identity, so relocating the data directory
still resolves the replaced browser.

## Limitations

- An update requires an existing managed installation. With none, the command directs you to
  `yantra browser install` rather than installing one for you.
- There is no version, channel, or mirror argument, and no pinning, rollback, or selectable version
  history. One ready pointer names the only selectable managed installation.
- A failed transfer cannot resume — the upstream archive is removed on failure — so a network error
  near the end of the download costs the whole transfer again. The command states this before you
  accept.
- The CLI exposes no cancellation flag. Core API callers can cancel cooperatively; on Windows the
  final setup step is non-interruptible, so a cancellation can wait for that bounded phase before the
  process tree exits.
- `--dry-run` reports whether a newer build exists, not whether it will work on this host. Testing a
  browser is `yantra browser check`, documented in
  [Browser Selection and Diagnostics](browser-selection-and-diagnostics.md).
- Updating is never automatic and cannot be automated from inside Yantra. There is no setting to make
  it run on a schedule, and the scheduler, daemon, and model tools cannot reach it.
